clue.text: Blake's definitive essayist?

definitions.note: possessive: read as the poem of William Blake's

parts.note: the definite article, the word that defines, is THE
Charles Lamb wrote the Essays of Elia

explanation.surface: A question about which essayist William Blake regarded as the definitive one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'definitive' is a play on the definite article. Blake's Songs of Innocence include a poem of this title.
explanation.definitionFit: A poem in William Blake's Songs of Innocence bears this title, so 'Blake's' points to his work.

clue.text: Rattle about Steele review

indicators.note: about signals that the letters of the word rattle are moved around

explanation.surface: Someone shakes up a review of Richard Steele's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges RATTLE. Richard Steele founded this periodical in 1709.
explanation.definitionFit: Steele's early-eighteenth-century periodical of essays and gossip carried this title.

clue.text: Choose artist for Greek drama

parts.note: to choose is to elect
RA, Royal Academician, is a standard abbreviation for an artist

explanation.surface: An instruction to pick a painter to design a Greek play.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophocles and Euripides each wrote a tragedy named after Agamemnon's daughter.

clue.text: Watercolour is all a queer mishmash

indicators.note: a mishmash is a jumble, so the letters of all a queer are mixed up

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a watercolour as a strange muddle.
explanation.definitionFit: This French borrowing names a painting done in transparent water-based paint.

clue.text: Essayist's beauties keep assignation, say

definitions.note: read as the plural essayists, the possessive mark printed as from OCR

indicators.note: keep means the first word holds the second within it

parts.note: belles are beautiful women

indicators.note: say signals that the word is given as it sounds rather than as spelt

parts.note: an assignation is a tryst, a lovers' meeting

explanation.surface: An essayist's lovely women keep a secret rendezvous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' gives a sound-alike of the lovers' word; 'keep' holds it within the beauties. The answer is plural, so 'Essayist's' must be read as essayists.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers of polished literary prose, such as essays, are called by this French term.

clue.text: Italian violinist, heartsick coming back

parts.note: the heart of something is its core

indicators.note: coming back means the word for sick is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: sick means ill

explanation.surface: An Italian fiddler returns home homesick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartsick' looks like one word of feeling, but the wordplay splits it; 'coming back' turns only the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: Arcangelo Corelli was a Baroque Italian composer and violinist.

clue.text: Evasive as Marvell's friend

definitions.meaning: Andrew Marvell's poem addresses his shy mistress

explanation.definitionFit: Coquettishly reticent; and the epithet Andrew Marvell gave the mistress of his famous poem.

clue.text: Bucolic, like Gay sports

definitions.meaning: John Gay wrote a georgic poem on country sports

explanation.definitionFit: Countryside-related, pastoral; and the adjective in the title of John Gay's 1713 poem about sports.

clue.text: Chesterton battle for the French children's entertainment

parts.note: le is French for the
a panto, pantomime, is a Christmas show for children

explanation.surface: A Chesterton battle scene staged as a French children's show.
explanation.walkthrough: PANTO is a British Christmas stage show for families. G. K. Chesterton wrote a poem about the 1571 naval battle.
explanation.definitionFit: G. K. Chesterton's 1911 poem celebrates the sea fight of 1571 against the Ottoman fleet.

clue.text: Somehow no undine undone in strange insinuation

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters of no undine are reached in some unstated arrangement

explanation.surface: A water-sprite is unaccountably ruined by a peculiar hint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' rearranges NO UNDINE; 'undone in strange' reinforces the anagram as padding.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblique suggestion or hint, usually disparaging, is this.

clue.text: Herbert creation offering assistance for the long haul?

definitions.text: offering assistance for the long haul?
definitions.meaning: a wheel and rope helping lift a heavy load

explanation.definitionFit: George Herbert wrote a poem of this title; the device it names eases hauling heavy loads.

clue.text: Mature start for Linklater's work

indicators.note: start for means only the opening stretch of the title is kept

parts.note: Eric Linklater wrote the novel Ripeness Is All

explanation.surface: A mature beginning for a Linklater book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start for' keeps the first five letters of the title Ripeness Is All, Eric Linklater's 1935 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: To mature is to grow ready, as fruit does.

clue.text: Stage direction for Dame Ngaio's villain

definitions.meaning: the instruction bringing an actor on

explanation.definitionFit: The script cue for an actor coming on; and the first word of Ngaio Marsh's title Enter a Murderer.

clue.text: Style Anne adapted in Victorian novel

indicators.note: adapted means the letters of style anne are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A stylish woman called Anne is turned into a Victorian novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Henry Wood's 1861 sensation novel, a byword for Victorian melodrama.

clue.text: "Dante believed that His kingdom would be established in the -will" (J. R. Lowell)

definitions.text: "Dante believed that His kingdom would be established in the -will" (J. R. Lowell)

parts.words: "Dante believed that His kingdom would be established in the -will" (J. R. Lowell)
parts.note: fill the gap in Lowell's essay on Dante with the word meaning given up or yielded

explanation.walkthrough: The gap takes a hyphenated adjective: a will given over to God.
explanation.definitionFit: Yielded or handed over, as a will given up to God.

clue.text: Barbara whose work has been an art of will

definitions.text: Barbara whose work has been an art of will

parts.words: Barbara whose work has been an art of will
parts.note: a best-selling novelist named Barbara whose books include Act of Will

explanation.walkthrough: 'art' is probably an OCR misread of 'act': Act of Will (1986) is one of her novels.
explanation.definitionFit: The popular novelist Barbara of this surname wrote A Woman of Substance and Act of Will.

clue.text: Ode thrice rewritten using double foot

indicators.note: rewritten means the letters of ode thrice are written out again in another order

explanation.surface: A poet revises an ode three times, using a double metrical foot.
explanation.definitionFit: In prosody, two trochees counted as a single compound unit.

clue.text: Condenses a poet

parts.note: Robert Bridges was Poet Laureate

explanation.definitionFit: Shortens a text while keeping its sense.

clue.text: Dickensian knight recalls Yorkist victory's vessels

parts.note: the Yorkists won the Battle of Barnet in 1471
kettles are vessels for boiling

explanation.surface: A Dickens knight remembers the pots of a battle in the Wars of the Roses.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet's kettles splits differently into the name of Sir Barnet Skettles of Dombey and Son.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Barnet Skettles is a pompous knight in Dombey and Son.

clue.text: Erect an adaptation and stage again

indicators.note: an adaptation reshapes the letters of erect an into a new form

explanation.surface: Putting up a new version of a play and staging it again.
explanation.definitionFit: To perform or act out once more.

clue.text: Play leading to mate by Beckett

definitions.meaning: the final phase of a chess game

explanation.definitionFit: The final phase of a chess game before checkmate; and the title of a Samuel Beckett play.

clue.text: Ibsen playshirt for chancellor

parts.note: Brand is an 1865 verse play by Henrik Ibsen
T, as in T-shirt

explanation.surface: An Ibsen play shirt for a German chancellor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playshirt' is an OCR run-together of 'play, shirt'.
explanation.definitionFit: Willy Brandt was West German Chancellor from 1969 to 1974.

clue.text: Idle aside wrongly quoted, yet highly regarded

indicators.note: wrongly quoted means the letters of idle aside are given in a mistaken order

explanation.surface: A careless remark misquoted, yet still admired.
explanation.definitionFit: Regarded as perfect, thought of as an ideal.

clue.text: Miss Bennet from ancient kingdom?

definitions.meaning: the youngest Bennet sister in Pride and Prejudice
the realm of Croesus in Asia Minor

explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's youngest Bennet sister; and the ancient realm of Croesus in Asia Minor.

clue.text: One of the last ones, perhaps, to win the Booker

definitions.text: One of the last ones, perhaps, to win the Booker

parts.words: One of the last ones, perhaps, to win the Booker
parts.note: Graham Swift won the Booker with Last ...; one of those is a single item

explanation.walkthrough: Graham Swift's Last Orders won the 1996 Booker Prize; last orders is the pub's final call for drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A single request, like one of the last ones called at a pub.

clue.text: Piano designed by John Dos Passos?

definitions.meaning: Dos Passos wrote the novel The ... Design

explanation.definitionFit: A large concert piano; and the adjective before Design in a Dos Passos novel title.

clue.text: A walk on the water from Brideshead figure

parts.note: a march is a walk
the main is the open sea

explanation.surface: A stroll on the water by someone from Brideshead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' joins the pieces. Lord Marchmain is Sebastian's father in Brideshead Revisited.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Marchmain is the head of the Flyte family in Evelyn Waugh's novel.

clue.text: Encyclopedist gives a thousand directions

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
E, east, is a compass direction, twice

explanation.surface: An encyclopedist gives a thousand instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Mee compiled The Children's Encyclopaedia.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Mee edited the Children's Encyclopaedia.

clue.text: "There's nothing — under heaven's eye / But hath his bound" (The Comedy of Errors)

definitions.text: "There's nothing — under heaven's eye / But hath his bound" (The Comedy of Errors)

parts.words: "There's nothing — under heaven's eye / But hath his bound" (The Comedy of Errors)
parts.note: fill Luciana's line from Shakespeare with the word meaning placed or located

explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adjective meaning placed or located.

clue.text: Most profound sequel, perhaps, to Benchley's 1976 success

definitions.meaning: Peter Benchley's 1976 novel The Deep; a sequel might go one deeper, then furthest

explanation.definitionFit: Superlative of profound; and a joking sequel title to Peter Benchley's novel The Deep.
